with_skill.expectation: Rejects the $15 sticker-pack tier sitting just below the $20 early-access tier, on the ground that sponsors offered a cheaper partial perk will take the cheaper one.
Notes that a no-perk gratitude tier placed below the converting tier is acceptable, so the cheap $1/$5 rungs are not themselves the problem.
Adds at least one company-priced tier at or above $250/month.
Identifies that a $50 top tier clears no corporate procurement process.
Prices at least one company tier against a stated placement audience figure (monthly views or equivalent traffic) rather than against generosity.
Names company tiers for the buyer, for example 'Team', 'Business' or 'Agency', instead of metal names like Gold or Platinum.
Keeps the live ladder to roughly three to five tiers and advises pricing for about two years ahead because the prices cannot later be edited.
Recommends employment - open-source time written into a job - or a commercial revenue model as the primary route to a salary-shaped number.
Positions sponsorship as a supplement rather than the primary instrument for this goal.
Asks clarifying questions one at a time rather than delivering the whole interview as a block.
Warns against publishing a $7,200 funding goal, since a goal stuck at a low percentage for a year reads as a project nobody supports.
Warns that switching an organization to invoiced billing cancels its existing sponsorships, which then have to be re-established.
Notes that invoices are payable within 30 days, or that the invoiced sponsor agreement runs three years before renewal.
Names the organization-account fee structure: up to 6%, being 3% credit-card processing plus a 3% service fee, with the credit-card portion removed under invoiced billing.

Works through the payable checklist: a legal entity or explicit contractor arrangement, the payer's expected tax form, ability to issue a numbered invoice, bank details for transfer, and a named beneficiary.
Notes that fiscal hosts generally charge 3-10% of funds received, with Open Source Collective at 10%.
Suggests raising the ask above $400/month given dependence across three named services, rather than accepting the first number offered.
Warns that a fiscal host is itself a continuity risk and recommends writing the exit-and-transfer plan before it is needed.
Recommends logging Northvale's budget month and opening the renewal conversation a full cycle ahead.
States the scale problem concretely - monthly calls at around 140 sponsors consume a working week or more per month.
Notes that the ten-times multiplier is a stress test, not a measured growth rate or forecast.

States the reward efficiency order, leading with README or docs placement ahead of badges and thank-you posts, early access, private repositories or office hours, and monthly calls or priority support last.
Refuses to gate the documentation needed to use the library.
Requires a genuinely useful free path, linked from the documentation, as the discovery route into the paid tier.
Recommends shipping gated content on a cadence, since a one-off gated release buys one month of sponsorship while a batch shipped with each release buys a subscription.
Tells the maintainer to budget production time for the gated content.
Tells the maintainer to check licence and employer constraints before gating anything derived from work someone else owns.
Notes that sponsorware is among the best-converting rewards on record and among the most expensive to keep delivering.
Applies the ten-times sponsor-count cost test to the ongoing gated-content commitment.
Recommends checking the OpenSSF Scorecard 'Maintained' score and fixing commit and release cadence before pitching if it reads dormant.
Puts a funding link within about two clicks of every surface users already touch: repository sponsor button, README, docs footer, release notes.
Turns the three Series-B startups into named outreach targets, recording the lockfile and issue evidence per company.
Does not treat sponsorship page views as the success metric, measuring conversion per surface instead.
Runs the four qualifying gates before drafting: licence, who can be paid, geography, and maturity or scope.
States that a grant is a fixed-term contract with an eligibility gate in front and a reporting duty behind, not a larger sponsor.
Recommends running the grant lane alongside a sponsorship program rather than instead of it.
Does not begin drafting application prose before the eligibility gates are settled.
Raises the post-award reporting and compliance admin as a recurring cost to budget against the maintainer's available hours.
Notes the 500,000 euro lifetime cap per recipient.
Rejects $5,000 as a first goal from a $210/month base and recommends a first goal that closes this quarter.
States that a completed goal is worth more than an ambitious one stuck at a low percentage for a year.
Notes that only one goal can run at a time.
Converts the goal into units a reader recognises - a maintenance day a week, a named infrastructure or code-signing bill, a dated deliverable - rather than a bare number.
Does not simply configure the $5,000 amount goal as asked.
Recommends publishing the boundary alongside the tiers rather than handling it privately per sponsor.
Keeps the sponsor list, the roadmap and the review queue as separate artefacts.
Recommends stating a conflict-of-interest rule naming which sponsors would be refused and who decides.
States the shape efficiency order out loud: visibility ahead of gratitude, ahead of retainer, ahead of access.
Emits separate orderings for value and effort rather than collapsing them into a single blended rank.
Names what the efficiency order starves - the retainer, the only shape that reaches salary-shaped income - and states the conditions that would promote it.
Seeks explicit agreement on the chosen shape before pricing any tier.
States that visibility delivery costs roughly an hour per sponsor for a logo commit and a placement check, which fits inside the stated ceiling.
States that the 50% line comes from freelance client-concentration practice and is a self-set threshold rather than an open-source funding norm.
Discards the $31,800 cumulative total as the wrong measure and asks for recurring monthly amount with its trend over six months instead.
Asks for the sponsor count split between individual and company sponsors.
Asks for monthly churn, the median tier, and the top sponsor's share of income.
Names the review cadence as 90 days and then quarterly.
Measures conversion from each surface carrying the funding link rather than page views.
Routes the user to the company-side sibling skill samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-sponsors-brand-strategy.
Stops rather than continuing into the maintainer workflow.
Confirms the payable prerequisites before sending: entity or contractor arrangement, tax form, numbered invoice, bank details.
Identifies that outreach only wins the judgement-based strategic sponsorship mechanism, and that dependency-share, employee-nominated funds and foundation or pledge membership are won differently.
Notes that Open Source Pledge members commit more than $2,000 per employed developer per year, so budget already exists looking for legible recipients.
Offers a one-page prospectus rather than a slide deck, including the section on what sponsorship does not buy.
Plans the renewal: logs the budget month and sends a short proof-of-value note each quarter.
